system.summary: Syllabic number table. 1-8 are a e i o r s t u; a ten is a consonant alone; XY with Y from 1 to 5 is consonant + a e i o u, and each row has one consonant for the plain group and another for the underlined group (g/r, l/s, m/t, n/v, p/z). Underlined single figures and tens are words (non, in, il, che, con, per, -ment-, stato, tutto). An x-shaped sign adds h. A stroke above a group doubles the consonant or marks an accent. Numbers of 100 and over are codes for names, titles and common words. Dates are written in clear as underlined numerals.

diacritics.note: an underline changes the value of a group; a short stroke above doubles the consonant or marks an accent; small raised numerals give plural endings on codes

system.doubled_letters: written once, or marked by a stroke above the group
system.notes: distinct_symbols counts the distinct groups (number plus underline) in the nine letters. nomenclator.entries counts the distinct numbers of 100 and over seen; none is counted read, including six with a value in the key and two with a value from the 1726 gloss.

prior_solution.where: Two sibling letters (Starhemberg to Riva, 27 Feb and 6 Mar 1726, cc. 5-10 and 19-20) carry a contemporary interlinear decipherment; the nine letters here carry none. Priority for the nine is NOT established: Lindgren, 'Gioseffo Riva (1682-1739), a Diplomatic Arbiter of buon gusto in the London of George I', Il Saggiatore musicale 23/2 (2016), 277-374, uses the Starhemberg file (it cites a letter of 13 March 1726 at p. 353, per Stefani) and was not seen (not open access). Lindgren and Timms 2003 (searched): no cipher passage, none of these letters.

No reading by a person without AI.

solution.what: Keyword harvest of the Estense catalogue (128 records with 'cifra'); the Starhemberg letters of 27 Feb and 6 Mar 1726 found to carry an interlinear decipherment over groups that look like the unsolved Selvatico 1722 letters.
Starhemberg, 20 Mar 1726 (unglossed): 409 groups transcribed and frozen before any key for this system existed.
Key K2 read off the glosses of the two sibling letters: a syllabic table with a plain and an underlined consonant per row. Seven rows were filled by table regularity without a gloss.

K2 applied to the 20 Mar 1726 letter and to another contributor's frozen transcriptions of the Selvatico 1722 letters: Italian in both; 0 of 5,000 shuffled keys as good. First count for 20 Mar 1726, 344 of 409 (84.11%), since withdrawn: three clear dates were counted as cipher and three groups were decoded by an unstated fallback.

Outside red-team review (not Anthropic models): the 1726 decode reproduced under stated rules; 53 of 136 lines of the 1722 letters decoded differently because the parser rules were unstated. A parser contract was then written before any further decode.
Own transcription of the four 1722 letters from full-size images (not blind: the other contributor's passes and K2 had been seen), frozen before decoding.

K3: 15 rows changed or added from context in the 1722 letters, each with two or more contexts (8_ per, 10_ -ment-, 70_ tutto, 53 gi, 54 go, 55 gu, 60_ si, 40_ stato, 01 qua, and six codes); the seven unglossed rows of K2 removed. Four 1722 letters: 1,273 of 1,436 units (88.65%); 0 of 5,000 shuffled keys.

Blind second transcription of the four 1722 letters by a separate session, frozen before any key or earlier transcription was opened: 1,390 of 1,441 aligned groups the same (96.46%); under K3, 1,237 of 1,432 (86.38%). 33 disagreements adjudicated on crops.

K3 frozen, then applied once and unchanged to newly transcribed letters: Selvatico's two undated letters (189 of 224), Starhemberg's secretary 19 Feb 1727 (84 of 97), Olivazzi 17 Apr 1725 (pass A 259 of 376). 0 of 5,000 shuffled keys on each, except the 48-unit letter alone (44 of 5,000).
Olivazzi: blind second transcription at full scale (268 of 378), 27 disagreements adjudicated on crops, consensus 278 of 377 (73.74%).
Sweep of Riva's other correspondents in the Estense catalogue for more letters in this table: 398 records viewed in full, none found; 111 not checked.

Check by Daniel Bourdeau on the five issues: decoders written from the keys reproduce the decodes, his own shuffled-key controls 0 of 5,000, 87 of 87 groups of the 1726 letter agree with the image. Errors of ours he found: the clear dates and the K2 fallback in #425, '56 repairs' is 15 key rows, #433 not re-read on the consensus. The Starhemberg letters fit Conrad Sigmund, not Guido.

For this folder: 20 Mar 1726 redone with the dates as clear text and one decode with K3, no fallback: 371 of 406 before reading, 351 of 406 (86.45%) after 20 downgrades; the reading now runs to the end. Olivazzi reading and English checked against the consensus decode. Every unit not read listed.

Lindgren 2016 (Il Saggiatore musicale 23/2) looked for: not open, not seen; known at second hand to cite a Starhemberg letter of 13 Mar 1726. Lindgren and Timms 2003 and Stefani searched through a fetch tool: no cipher passage and none of these letters. Modena-side archives not checked.

Statistical validation (docs/_validate.py): 2175 tokens, 96 types, it-modern order 4: reading -1.96 per letter; random keys -4.179 (z 11.0); key annealed onto shuffled ciphertext best -2.705 (mean -2.71, z 128.6); annealer on the real text -2.479. Verdict: pass.

Integration check: scripts/build.py rerun, every count reproduces (2175 of 2540; per letter as filed); a second decoder written from key.tsv and the transcriptions alone agrees on 97 of 97 groups (19 Feb 1727) and 406 of 406 (20 Mar 1726); RFC 3161 replies read (K3 21:30 GMT, 1727 22:04, Olivazzi 22:13, 11 Nov); all 97 groups of c. 23r agree with the Estense image; K3 gives no language on the 31 May 1721 letter, so the 1720-21 letters are a separate target (starhemberg1721). Rough word-level count from the readings: about 74% (estimate, not the headline).

Limits found at integration: K3's 15 rows were made on the four 1722 letters (their 88.7% is in-sample; 90 of the 2175 counted groups use a K3-changed row); K2 cannot be re-derived from the files (ten gloss pairs kept, the two glossed letters not transcribed); row 5 (plain 51 and 52) unsettled; the order of events is shown by the time stamps, which cannot show that nobody looked earlier.

validation.notes: claimed per-occurrence score -1.967; polyphony 0.073; 365 unread tokens left out; annealer on the real text from random keys reached -2.479

texts.label: Benedetto Selvatico Estense (Modena) to Giuseppe Riva (London), '10 Xbre'
texts.summary: From Modena. In clear: he never believes the Congress will be held; Rangoni is in Paris against his advice and at great cost. In cipher: he is sorry to say the contrary of what was asked, because someone (the person asking to come home, or Riva) will soon go on to Paris or to a coded place; orders from the Duke will follow by this or the next post. Context: the run-up to the Congress of Cambrai.

texts.label: Benedetto Selvatico Estense (Modena) to Giuseppe Riva (London), '2 Genaro'
texts.summary: From Modena, almost all in cipher. No letters from a coded person (probably Riva) by this post. The Princes of Modena have come back from Rome with Cardinal de Rohan, dined at Modena and gone on to Reggio; the Cardinal, held there by gout, is said to be about to leave for France. The Duke seems to mean to post the coded person elsewhere and will write.

texts.label: Benedetto Selvatico Estense (Vienna) to Giuseppe Riva (London), 10 June 1722
texts.summary: From Vienna. He asks Riva for what only Riva can tell: whether George I has been won for the Duke of Modena's claims. The ministers in Vienna say that power must take up the Duke's cause at the congress, but fear it will not commit itself; this is at odds with what Modena writes. He needs a sure answer quickly, to persuade Vienna if it is good and to warn the Duke not to hope too much if it is bad.

texts.label: Benedetto Selvatico Estense (Vienna) to Giuseppe Riva (London), 29 July 1722
texts.summary: The state of the Duke's affairs at Vienna: everything hangs on the congress and on the help two coded powers (England and France, proposed) give there. Riva should keep George I well disposed and commit him to the indemnity, for which a coded principal (the Emperor, proposed) has declared he will give every assistance if those two do not drop it. The Naples credits sleep until details come from Modena. The ministers are divided, most favour the Duke.

texts.label: Benedetto Selvatico Estense (Vienna) to Giuseppe Riva (London), 8 August 1722
texts.summary: The longest letter. The Duke's chief concern is the indemnity for the damage his States suffered in the war; it depends on the congress (Cambrai). The Emperor (proposed value) has fenced so far. Pressed, the ministers have now told the truth: he will never promote the claim and wishes it kept quiet, because once it is raised the other side will raise many other points, and may say something about Mirandola (spelt out), a point that cost the State so much money. He will support the claim warmly if the Duke or another power raises it, but will not be the principal. It remains to weigh harm against gain and to choose who should raise it.

texts.label: Benedetto Selvatico Estense (Vienna) to Giuseppe Riva (London), 12 August 1722
texts.summary: He is upset at news of a move to have a coded place restored to Pico (the dispossessed Duke of Mirandola): the blow would be fatal. For this reason the Emperor (proposed) will not propose the indemnity, 'so as not to wake sleeping dogs'. Frankly, this court is not to be trusted much: it seeks only its own interest. What a coded person wrote about there being no instructions to assist the Duke is false.

texts.label: Giorgio Olivazzi (Milan) to Giuseppe Riva, 17 April 1725
texts.summary: From Milan. A party of opponents, named in code, has always worked to obstruct him; honest men are few. After a year and a half a coded patron has had him recommended. The dispute is not about the payments at issue, that is the excuse: the aim is to keep him in bad repute and from advancement; they turned a coded authority against him and used the Inquisition. Then three interests of the Duke of Modena, one of which involves a proposal, under hand, to send an Archduchess. The least secure reading of the nine: many coded persons, four stretches unread, a page edge hidden.

texts.label: Count Starhemberg (Vienna; filed under Guido, content fits Conrad Sigmund) to Giuseppe Riva (London), 20 March 1726
texts.summary: He thanks Riva for three letters (19 and 22 February, 6 March), says most of the news reached him earlier from other correspondents, and asks him to report punctually on the court and general affairs. A yearly 100 pounds sterling is in question. Riva and 'the friend in Holland' (value from the 1726 gloss) may count on at least a couple of hundred in fees between them this year, part from Starhemberg's own pocket, and, for news of consequence, on reward and an Imperial favour. The Duke of Modena will find his account in it if he and his ministers stay good Imperials. Context: paid intelligence for the Emperor's envoy from the Modenese agent in London, during the Vienna/Hanover alliance crisis. The middle of the letter has holes.

texts.label: Count Starhemberg's secretary (Vienna) to Giuseppe Riva (London), 19 February 1727
texts.summary: French clear text about a Baron d'Eisenberg's courtship is cover. The cipher begins where the lady's name should stand: everything so far is feigned; His Excellency asks Riva to watch closely what passes in affairs, particularly with Palm (the Emperor's resident in London), as to his conduct now and later, and what measures the British court takes. Palm was expelled from London the next month.
